1→![ALT](/media/images/gemm-hierarchy-with-epilogue-no-labels.png "Complete CUDA GEMM decomposition")
     2→
     3→# Python packages associated with CUTLASS
     4→
     5→This directory contains Python packages that are associated with CUTLASS:
     6→
     7→* `cutlass_cppgen`: the CUTLASS Python interface, which enables one to compile and run CUTLASS kernels from within Python. Note that this was previously named `cutlass`, but was renamed to disambiguate with the CuTe Python DSL.
     8→* `cutlass_library`: utilities used for enumerating and emitting C++ code for CUTLASS kernels
     9→
    10→## CUTLASS Python Interface
    11→
    12→The CUTLASS Python interface enables one to compile and run CUTLASS operations from within Python.
    13→
    14→```python
    15→import cutlass
    16→import numpy as np
    17→
    18→plan = cutlass.op.Gemm(element=np.float16, layout=cutlass.LayoutType.RowMajor)
    19→A, B, C, D = [np.ones((1024, 1024), dtype=np.float16) for i in range(4)]
    20→plan.run(A, B, C, D)
    21→```
    22→
    23→### Overview
    24→
    25→The CUTLASS Python interface prioritizes ease of use.
    26→It has the following features that support this goal.
    27→
    28→* It presents high-level interfaces for operators, that require only few parameters.
    29→* It selects sensible default configurations for an operator given the parameters that have been specified.
    30→* It enumerates configurations for users that are known to work in a given setting.
    31→* It favors emitting descriptive Python run-time exceptions instead of C++ compile-time errors, where possible.
    32→* It simplifies exporting CUTLASS kernels to framework extensions (e.g., PyTorch CUDA extensions).
    33→
    34→#### Non-goals
    35→The CUTLASS Python interface does not intend to:
    36→
    37→1. select optimal kernel configurations,
    38→2. act as a fast container for CUTLASS kernels, or
    39→3. act as a Python-to-CUDA-kernel just-in-time (JIT) compilation engine.
    40→
    41→Regarding selection of optimal kernel configurations,
    42→the interface favors ease-of-use over maximum configurability.
    43→Thus, its default selections for operator parameters may
    44→not achieve the highest possible performance in all scenarios. Users wishing to achieve the highest performance possible should either
    45→
    46→* select parameters by profiling different combinations of them, or
    47→* use a library such as [cuBLAS](https://developer.nvidia.com/cublas)
    48→  that contains heuristics for selecting kernels.
    49→
    50→Regarding acting as a fast container for CUTLASS kernels:
    51→the interface does not strive to minimize overhead in its Python functions surrounding the running of a kernel.
    52→Those wishing to deploy a CUTLASS kernel should either
    53→
    54→* use the C++ emitted by the Python interface directly, or
    55→* use one of the CUTLASS emitters for automatically creating a framework extension for the kernel (e.g., a PyTorch CUDA extension).
    56→
    57→Regarding acting as a Python-to-CUDA-kernel JIT compilation engine:
    58→the interface enables use of CUTLASS in Python code.
    59→It can be used by frameworks for JIT compiling
    60→Python to CUDA kernels, but does not set out to be such a framework.
    61→
    62→#### Comparison to PyCUTLASS
    63→
    64→The CUTLASS Python interface builds atop CUTLASS's [PyCUTLASS](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/tree/v3.0.0/tools/library/scripts/pycutlass) library. PyCUTLASS enables
    65→one to declare, compile, and run GEMMs, convolutions, and grouped GEMM operators with nearly the same configuration
    66→space as CUTLASS's C++ interface. While this flexibility enables one to achieve the similar levels of functionality
    67→as available in CUTLASS's C++ interface, it comes with the burden of needing to specify many configuration parameters
    68→to operators -- similar to what one must do in specifying template parameters to operations in CUTLASS's C++ interface.
    69→
    70→In contrast, the CUTLASS Python interface aims to provide a higher-level API for declaring, emitting, and compiling
    71→kernels that does not require exhaustively defining template parameters.
    72→
    73→### Current functionality
    74→The CUTLASS Python interface currently supports the following operations:
    75→* GEMMs
    76→* GEMMs with fused elementwise epilogues (e.g., ReLU) (for pre-SM90 kernels)
    77→* Stream K swizzling (for pre-SM90 kernels)
    78→* Grouped GEMM (for pre-SM90 kernels)
    79→
    80→### Getting started
    81→We recommend using the CUTLASS Python interface via an [NGC PyTorch Docker container](https://catalog.ngc.nvidia.com/orgs/nvidia/containers/pytorch):
    82→
    83→```bash
    84→docker run --gpus all -it --rm nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:23.08-py3 -p 8888:8888
    85→```
    86→
    87→The CUTLASS Python interface has been tested with CUDA 11.8, 12.0, and 12.1 on Python 3.8 and 3.9.
    88→
    89→#### Optional environment variables
    90→
    91→Prior to installing the CUTLASS Python interface, one may optionally set the following environment variables:
    92→
    93→* `CUTLASS_PATH`: the path to the cloned CUTLASS repository
    94→* `CUDA_INSTALL_PATH`: the path to the installation of CUDA
    95→
    96→If these environment variables are not set, the installation process will infer them to be the following:
    97→
    98→* `CUTLASS_PATH`: either one directory level above the current directory (i.e., `$(pwd)/..`) if installed locally or in the `source` directory of the location in which `cutlass_library` was installed
    99→* `CUDA_INSTALL_PATH`: the directory holding `/bin/nvcc` for the first version of `nvcc` on `$PATH` (i.e., `which nvcc | awk -F'/bin/nvcc' '{print $1}'`)
   100→
   101→**NOTE:** The version of `cuda-python` installed must match the CUDA version in `CUDA_INSTALL_PATH`.
   102→
   103→#### Installation
   104→
   105→Stable releases of the CUTLASS Python interface are available via the `nvidia-cutlass` PyPI package. Any other packages with the name `cutlass` are not affiliated with NVIDIA CUTLASS.
   106→```bash
   107→pip install nvidia-cutlass
   108→```
   109→
   110→The CUTLASS Python interface can also be installed from source by navigating to the root of the CUTLASS directory and performing
   111→```bash
   112→pip install .
   113→```
   114→
   115→If you would like to be able to make changes to the CUTLASS Python interface and have them reflected when using the interface, perform:
   116→```bash
   117→pip install -e .
   118→```
   119→
   120→To test that your installation was successful, you can run:
   121→```python
   122→import cutlass
   123→import numpy as np
   124→
   125→plan = cutlass.op.Gemm(element=np.float16, layout=cutlass.LayoutType.RowMajor)
   126→A, B, C, D = [np.ones((128, 128), dtype=np.float16) for i in range(4)]
   127→plan.run(A, B, C, D)
   128→```
   129→
   130→### Deep learning framework CUDA extensions
   131→The CUTLASS Python interface provides utilities for exporting a CUTLASS kernel to a deep learning framework CUDA extensions. Currently, PyTorch CUDA extensions can be exported, but a similar pattern could be applied for other frameworks as well. An example of this is provided [here](/examples/python/02_pytorch_extension_grouped_gemm.ipynb).
   132→
   133→Currently, the following operations can be exported to a PyTorch CUDA extension:
   134→* GEMM
   135→* Grouped GEMM
   136→* Conv2d
   137→
   138→### Examples
   139→
   140→Jupyter notebook examples of using the CUTLASS Python interface are located in [examples/python](/examples/python).
   141→
   142→To launch these notebooks from this directory, run:
   143→```bash
   144→jupyter-lab ../examples/python
   145→```
   146→
   147→### Building documentation
   148→
   149→The CUTLASS Python interface uses [Sphinx](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/) for documentation.
   150→
   151→Building the documentation requires additional packages.  The following commands will install them.
   152→```bash
   153→sudo apt-get install pandoc
   154→pip install --upgrade Sphinx furo pandoc myst-parser sphinx-copybutton nbsphinx nbsphinx-link sphinx-inline-tabs
   155→```
   156→
   157→To build documentation, you must first have installed the CUTLASS Python interface via the
   158→[installation instructions](#installation).
   159→
   160→Documentation can then be built via the following commands.
   161→```bash
   162→sphinx-apidoc -o docs_src/source/ cutlass/ cutlass/backend*
   163→cd docs_src
   164→make html
   165→mv _build/* ../docs
   166→```
   167→
   168→## CUTLASS library package
   169→
   170→[cutlass_library](/python/cutlass_library) contains utilities for enumerating and emitting CUTLASS C++ kernels.
   171→It is used by the CUTLASS CMake system to construct a library of kernels that can be profiled using the CUTLASS profiler.
   172→
   173→To install the `cutlass_library` package, run
   174→```bash
   175→python setup_library.py develop --user
   176→```
   177→
   178→Alternatively, `cutlass_library` will automatically be installed if you install the CUTLASS Python interface package.
   179→
